messages.subject_clean: procD.pgls error: data matrix missing taxa present on tree
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm tying to do a phylogenetic ANOVA on some linear (not gm) morphological measurements using the procD.pgls function and I keep getting an error saying that the data matrix is missing some taxa present on the tree. I have triple-checked everything and my data row names and tree tip labels are EXACTLY the same character strings in EXACTLY the same order.

Is there something I'm missing? The same set of measurements and phylogeny have worked with the pgls function in caper, so unless I'm going crazy the row names and the tree names are the same. Does anyone have any thoughts?

My code here:

> #this is my data previously arranged so the row order matches the order of names in the tip.label vector of my tree
> mC1 <- as.data.frame(maleC1_ordered[,1:15])
> rownames(mC1) <- mC1$spp
>
> #geomorph data frame
> gdf_mC1 <- geomorph.data.frame(mC1, phy = treeMale)
>
> #phylogenetic ANOVA with a continuous response variable LDA and categorical predictor fightStyle
> mC1_model <- procD.pgls(LDA ~ fightStyle, phy = phy, data = gdf_mC1)
>
> #This is the response I get when trying to run the procD.pgls:
> #Error in procD.pgls(LDA ~ fightStyle, phy = phy, data = gdf_mC1) :
> #Data matrix missing some taxa present on the tree.

Thanks for your help!

-Abby

Abby,

Often when this happens, something like an extra space can make it difficult to see the difference between tree tip labels and specimen names.  I recommend doing something like the following, assuming using your data are a matrix,Y (adjust this if they are a vector or array):

match(rownames(Y), phy$tip.label)

You can also do this switching the order around.  If you find any NA values, then it means the spelling differs between the two sets of names (even if they look EXACTLY the same).

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Nick, your superimposed data look OK, although you are the best person to judge that, being more familiar with the system and digitizing scheme.

You can use bilat.symmetry to obtain the symmetric shapes, but beware that in that case you are eliminating biological asymmetries in addition to any user-introduced effects. Just a matter of definition, nothing wrong with doing that, to my view, if you are not interested in asymmetry as a biological pattern.

Hope this helps!

Antigoni

messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I've generated a PCA plot using plottangentspace from shape data from for all 15 populations in my study. However, as you can see in the attached image, the legend is not showing all 15 populations. Can someone please help me make my legend functional, I haven't found any mention of moving or altering legends in plottangentspace in this forum, online or in the relevant help file. I have tried using the normal graphical alterations for the plot function but have had no success.

As a side note, something I struggled with was to change the default colour settings for plottangentspace to show more than just 8 colours (being new to R).
If anyone is in the same position, using the code below is how I generated my unique 15 colours (there are of course many different ways to do this).

#Create colour vector
colours<-c("gold","blue","firebrick1","gray0","chocolate1","chartreuse","blueviolet","gray","goldenrod4","deeppink","darkslategrey","burlywood4","azure3","darkorange","dimgray")

#find more colours in  R here http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~tzheng/files/Rcolor.pdf

palette(colours) #this sets the collection of colours just defined as the new default colour palette

#Can now just run plottangentspace as normal and it will show groups in the colour of the order of the colour vector I just defined ie 1st group will be gold, 2nd group will be blue, third group firebrick1 (red) and so on. This will work up until 15 groups when the colours will start repeating (I only have 15 populations in my study).

Cheers
Angus

Angus,

Try this. I hope this solves your problem.

#PCA Plot
pca.plot <- function(x,y,xlab,ylab,col) {
  plot(x,y,xlab = xlab,ylab = ylab,cex = 0.75)
  legend('bottomleft',legend = levels(col),col = rainbow(length(levels(col))),pch=19,cex = 0.75)
  orders <- levels(col)
  ord.col <- rainbow(length(orders))
  for(i in 1:length(orders)) {
    grp <- which(col == orders[i])
    points(x[grp],y[grp],pch = 19,col = ord.col[i])
  }
}

pca.plot(PCA$pc.scores[,1],PCA$pc.scores[,2],xlab = xlab, ylab = ylab, col = Data$Group)

Cheers,

Mohamad

messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I would like to compare diparities of different vertebral regions (cervical, thoracic...) with a different number of landmarks for a set of species. We have computed two different sets of Procrustes ANOVA (procD.lm):
(i) using vertebral identity (e.g., cervical3*cervical4*....) as a factor for each region (cervical,thoracic...).
(ii) using species (species1*species2*species3) as a factor for each region.
Our goal is to compare if morphological variability for each region is explained by interspecific or intra-regional varibility -i.e., if differences between vertebrae for each region (e.g., cervical3-cervical7 or thoracic1-thoracic11) are larger than the differences between species (e.g., cervical_species1-cervical_species11 or thoracic_species1-thoracic_species11 and so on).
To do this, we have computed the Zscore obtained from procD.lm from each Procustes ANOVA, but we are not sure if this is the best option of variability comparison. Moreovoer, we do not know how to compare it statistically, we guess that a bootstrap procedure is needed here but I wonder if you could give any insight on how to reshufle the data.
Best wishes and thank you very much in advance,
borja
PS: Please, note that we cannot digitize the same number of landmarks in all the vertebrae as we lose a lot of morphological information in some regions.

Are you performing GPA on all vertebrae coordinates together?  If so, I’m not sure comparing disparities (Procrustes variances) among different vertebrae would make much sense as the GPA - not evolution - could be most responsible for variation in disparities among vertebrae with different densities of landmarks.

More generally, having different numbers of landmarks for different vertebrae, both within an individual and across species, makes it hard to think of a logical comparative analysis.  Maybe somebody else will have a good idea, but just be careful with interpreting disparity in parts of configurations that were influenced by GPA performed on entire configurations.

Best,
Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] Calculating trait disparity
messages.body_plain:
Nick,

In the form of a script,

fit <- procD.pgls(coords ~ 1, phy = myTree, …)
dist(fit$pgls.residuals)

By fitting a model with only an intercept, the distance matrix among species residuals is the same as the distance matrix among species values, after accounting for phylogeny.  If you rather use PC scores than coordinates,

PCA <- prcomp(fit$pgls.residuals)
dist(PCA$x)

You should get comparable results, regardless.

Cheers!
Mike

messages.body_plain:
Charles,

That is hard to trouble shoot, though having an R2 of 0.998 for CSize is rather suspicious. The comparison you made though is uncontrolled because different datasets are used. I would first look at a nonphylogenetic analysis using the same data as in the PGLS analysis (ie, use procD.lm).  If you have similar R2 for CSize, then one of two things is possible.

One: you have crazy-different sizes across species and these are perfectly correlated with their average shapes.

Two: something in your procedures of obtaining average shapes, average sizes, or both is incorrect, causing a spurious and very high R2.

I suggest you investigate via the non-PGLS approach first and then check all of your pre-analysis computations of averages.

> data("plethspecies")
> plethspecies$land[,,1] <- plethspecies$land[,,1] * 10 # make one really large specimen

I wish to study shape of human nose. I have a 3D .ply file for human face. I digitized 11 landmarks around the nose using Landmark Editor and imported the coordinates into R. I plotted the coordinates on the .ply file in R using the command:

#Import the template .ply file
tmpply <- read.ply("E:\\Research\\GM\\3D started\\Samples\\a\\170113141933.ply", ShowSpecimen=T)

plot3d(mydata[1:5,,2], type = "s", radius = 1.5, col = "red", aspect = FALSE, add = T)

plot3d(mydata[6:11,,2], type = "s", radius = 1.5, col = "green", aspect = FALSE, add = T)

I ge the following figure:

The landmarks lie exactly on the surface mesh, as expected.

I wish to add 100 sliding surface semilandmarks onto the nose, so I used the following command:

buildtemplate(spec = tmpply, fixed = mydata[,,2], surface.sliders = 100, ptsize=1)

where mydata[,,2] is the coordinate for the 11 landmarks digitized on this template. I was returned the following image:

Obviously, the automatically generated sliding surface semilandmarks do no lie on the surface mesh! What should be done so that all automatically generated sliding surface semilandmarks lie on the surface mesh? In addition, is there a way to constrain those surface semilandmarks to the nasal region?

Best regards,

Patrick

The procD.lm and procD.pgls examples all use geomorph data frames, so how to do this can be inferred through those examples.

Thank you very much!
